title: The Most Common House Extension Mistakes (and How to Avoid Them)
metaTitle: The Most Common House Extension Mistakes to Avoid
description: The extension mistakes that come up again and again, from posts in the middle of the kitchen to skipped rooflights and mid-build changes, and how to avoid them.
author: Jason Berry
coverAlt: Well-matched brick rear extension with bifold doors and rooflights, an example of getting the structure and the light right
coverCaption: Most expensive extension mistakes are made at the design stage, not on site: shrinking the steel, forgetting the light, or quoting a different job.

blocks.text: The most common extension mistakes are rarely dramatic. They are small decisions made too quickly: shrinking the structural opening to save a little money, forgetting to design in light, changing your mind once the builders are on site, and choosing a builder on price alone. Each is avoidable, and each is far cheaper to fix on paper than on site.

This guide runs through the mistakes that come up again and again, why they happen, what they cost, and how to sidestep them, so your extension turns out the way you pictured it rather than teaching you these lessons the hard way.
Shrinking the structural opening to save money

To create one bright, open room, you remove the load-bearing wall between the house and the extension, and the weight above goes onto a steel beam. The wider the opening, the bigger and more expensive the steel.

The mistake is shrinking that opening, or leaving a stub of wall or a supporting post in the middle, purely to fit a smaller, cheaper beam. It saves a modest sum at build time and leaves you looking at a column in the centre of your new kitchen, or a room that never quite feels open, for as long as you live there.

How to avoid it: decide the opening you actually want first, then price the steel to suit, rather than letting a cheaper beam dictate the room. It is one of the few extension costs you genuinely feel every single day, so it is the wrong place to economise. Our guide on open-plan living and steel beams explains how this works in detail.
Forgetting to design in light

blocks.alt: Kitchen extension with a wide run of sliding doors bringing garden light into the room
blocks.caption: A deep rear extension without rooflights or a lantern often leaves the middle of the original house dark.

blocks.text: This is the single most common regret, and it is entirely avoidable.

When you extend across the back of a house, the middle of the original room ends up several metres from any window and goes dark. When you fill in a side return, you build over the one place daylight reached the kitchen. Either way, without rooflights or a lantern designed in from the start, you end up with a bigger room that is gloomier than the smaller one you started with.

How to avoid it: treat rooflights and a lantern as part of the design, not an optional extra to be trimmed when the budget tightens. A run of rooflights over a side return, or a lantern over a kitchen island, is usually what makes the whole space work. It is the first thing people cut and the first thing they wish they had kept.

blocks.label: Common misconception
blocks.text: "A bigger room is automatically a better room." Not if it is dark. Floor area without light produces a space nobody wants to sit in. The extensions people love are the light ones, not simply the large ones, which is why glazing and rooflights earn their place in the budget.
Designing the space before thinking how you will use it

People often design an extension around how it looks on a plan, then discover it does not work in real life: the sink is miles from the hob, the dining table blocks the doors, there is nowhere sensible for the fridge, or the family room has no wall for the sofa.

How to avoid it: design the space around how you will actually live in it, before the walls go up. On a kitchen especially, the positions of the sink, hob and extractor drive the drainage and the ductwork, so they are expensive to move later. Working the layout through properly at the design stage, right down to where the furniture goes, costs nothing and saves a great deal.
Changing your mind once the build has started

Every change made after work begins, a moved wall, a different layout, an added rooflight, an upgraded finish, costs more than the same decision made on paper, often much more, and it adds time as well as money. Materials get reordered, work gets undone and redone, and the programme slips.

How to avoid it: make the decisions at the design stage, when they are nearly free, and lock the design down before work starts. It is fine to take longer over the design if it means fewer changes on site. The most expensive way to build an extension is to decide as you go.

blocks.label: Worth knowing
blocks.text: The cheapest changes are the ones made with a pencil. A decision altered at the design stage costs almost nothing; the same decision altered once the steel is in and the walls are up can cost hundreds or thousands and push the finish date back. Time spent getting the design right before the build is the best-value time in the whole project.
Choosing a builder on price alone
Gather three quotes and they will often differ by a surprising amount. The mistake is simply picking the lowest without understanding why it is lowest.

A cheaper quote has often, quietly, quoted a different job: a smaller structural opening, foundations that assume the ground will cope, no rooflights, no drainage diversion, no making good, or a lower specification, or it has left VAT off. None of that is visible if you are comparing two lump-sum totals.

How to avoid it: insist on itemised quotes, so you can see what the steel, the groundwork, the glazing and the finish each cost, and compare like with like. The lowest number is not the cheapest job if it leaves out things you will have to pay for later. Our guide on extension costs breaks down exactly where quotes differ.

blocks.label: Common misconception
blocks.text: "The cheapest quote saves me money." Only if it is quoting the same job. If the low quote has left out the underpinning your ground needs, or designed a post into your kitchen to shrink the steel, the saving is either an illusion you pay for later or a compromise you live with. Compare what is in the quotes, not just the totals.
Under-budgeting and leaving no contingency

Extensions run over budget less because the builder was expensive and more because the homeowner's budget never included everything in the first place. The commonly forgotten items: structural steel and its groundwork, rooflights, drainage, making good the garden, planning and building control fees, the kitchen and flooring on a kitchen extension, and VAT.

How to avoid it: build a realistic budget that includes those items from the start, and keep a contingency, commonly around ten per cent, for the genuine unknowns, especially anything below ground. An extension with no contingency is one bad surprise away from a stalled project.

blocks.label: Worth knowing
blocks.text: Always hold a contingency, and treat it as untouchable until the groundwork is done. The ground is where the real surprises live, and it is dug at the start, so if a surprise is coming it usually comes early. A contingency turns "the project stalled" into "we dealt with it and carried on".
Ignoring the ground until it is a problem

The foundations are the part of the job you cannot see when it is finished and the most expensive part to get wrong. Clay that moves near trees, soft or wet ground near water, made ground, old workings or a high water table can all mean deeper or more complex foundations, and finding that out mid-dig is where budgets and timelines derail.

How to avoid it: understand the ground before pricing and starting, not after. On a tricky or leafy plot, a proper look at the ground before work begins is protection, not an upsell, and a builder who wants to know what is under your extension before they quote is doing exactly the right thing.
Over-extending: losing the garden, the light or the ceiling price
More is not always better. Three versions of the same mistake:

Building out so far that you swallow most of the garden, trading inside space for outside space in a way that can actually reduce the home's appeal. Building so large that the extension darkens the original house or the garden. And spending on an extension so ambitious that it pushes the house past the ceiling price of the street, the most any home on that road can sell for, so you never recoup the cost.

How to avoid it: extend enough to transform the house, not so much that you lose what made it work. Keep a usable garden, keep the light, and if resale matters, know your street's ceiling before you spend. Our guide on whether an extension adds value covers the ceiling price in detail.
How to avoid all of them

Almost every mistake here shares a single root cause: rushing the design and the planning to get to the build. And almost every one is prevented the same way, by getting the design right, the budget honest and the builder chosen properly before anyone breaks ground.

This is where we come in, gently. We design and build extensions with one team from start to finish, so the design, the structure, the light and the budget are thought through together rather than falling between separate trades. faqs.q: What is the most common mistake people make with extensions?
faqs.a: Forgetting to design in light. Extending across the back of a house darkens the middle of the original room, and filling in a side return builds over the kitchen's main source of daylight. Without rooflights or a lantern designed in from the start, people end up with a bigger but gloomier room. It is the single most common regret and entirely avoidable.

faqs.q: Why do extension quotes vary so much, and how do I compare them?
faqs.a: Because cheaper quotes often quote a different job, a smaller structural opening, foundations that assume the ground will cope, or no rooflights, drainage or VAT. Insist on itemised quotes so you can compare what the steel, groundwork, glazing and finish each cost, rather than comparing two lump-sum totals. The lowest number is not the cheapest job if it leaves things out.

faqs.q: How much contingency should I budget for an extension?
faqs.a: A commonly used figure is around ten per cent of the project cost, held back for genuine unknowns, especially below ground where the real surprises live. Treat it as untouchable until the groundwork is complete. An extension with no contingency is one bad surprise away from stalling.

faqs.q: Why is changing my mind during the build so expensive?
faqs.a: Because work has to be undone and redone, materials reordered, and the programme slips. A decision made at the design stage is nearly free; the same decision made once the steel is in and the walls are up can cost far more and delay the finish. Locking the design down before work starts is the best way to control cost.

faqs.q: Can I make my extension too big?
faqs.a: Yes. Over-extending can swallow the garden, darken the original house, or push the home past the ceiling price of the street so the cost is never recouped. Extend enough to transform the house, but keep a usable garden and, if resale matters, stay mindful of what your street can command.

faqs.q: Why does the ground matter so much before I start?
faqs.a: The foundations are the part you cannot see when finished and the most expensive to get wrong. Clay that moves near trees, soft or wet ground, made ground or old workings can all mean deeper foundations, and discovering that mid-dig derails budgets and timelines. Understanding the ground before pricing prevents the most common overruns.

faqs.q: Should I choose the cheapest builder?
faqs.a: Not on price alone. Compare itemised quotes to see whether the cheapest is quoting the same job or a stripped-back one, and weigh reputation and how the builder communicates. A slightly higher quote for the job done properly usually beats a low one that leaves out steel, foundations or finishes you then pay for separately.

faqs.q: How do I avoid extension mistakes altogether?
faqs.a: Get the design, the budget and the builder right before you break ground. Design around how you will live in the space, design in light, lock the design down to avoid mid-build changes, budget for the hidden costs with a contingency, understand the ground, and choose a builder on an itemised quote and reputation rather than the lowest number. Most extension mistakes trace back to rushing this stage.
